newsitem.title: EGYPT: U.S.-jailed Egypt cleric's wife fears for his health.
newsitem.headline: U.S.-jailed Egypt cleric's wife fears for his health.

text.p: The wife of an Egyptian militant Moslem cleric sentenced in the United States to life in jail on bombing charges said on Saturday she feared for his health.

"I spoke to him for five minutes last month. He was very sick. He is blind and sits all day alone," Faten, the younger of Sheikh Omar Abdel-Rahman's two wives, told Reuters. "Visitors are prohibited. We're not allowed to send him anything."
Sheikh Omar was convicted in a 1995 trial of conspiracy to bomb New York landmarks and assassinate political leaders.

His lawyers told Reuters in New York on Friday the health of the cleric, who has long suffered from diabetes, asthma and a heart condition, had so deteriorated that his life could be in danger. They blamed U.S. regulations.

On Saturday the Arabic newspaper Al-Hayat quoted unnamed Egyptian sources as saying Egypt had recently refused a U.S. proposal to send Abdel-Rahman back to Egypt. A U.S. embassy spokesman told Reuters he had no information on the report.

"It sounds like the sheikh's condition is deteriorating and obviously could be life-threatening. He is having trouble breathing, suffering severe headaches, itching from allergies and has abdominal pain around his liver and kidneys," said one of his lawyers, former U.S. attorney general Ramsay Clark.
Clark is handling the appeal for Sheikh Omar.

U.S. prison authorities said he was being treated fairly under rules introduced in May 1996 for prisoners linked with terrorism. The rules restrict contact with a spouse to once a month, and Sheikh Omar can place calls only to his lawyers.
"Where is the freedom, human rights and democracy that we hear so much about in the U.S.? In Egypt at least I could visit him," Faten said by telephone from Fayoum, south of Cairo.

Clark said for more than a month Abdel-Rahman had been kept in virtual isolation in a damp cell in a federal prison in Missouri. He said the cleric had not been given tapes of readings from the Koran and other religious texts he sent.

Abdel-Rahman and nine others were convicted of conspiracy to carry out acts that included blowing up the United Nations, other New York City landmarks and plans to assassinate political leaders including Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak.

Egypt's government has accused him of leading Egypt's most violent group, al-Gama'a al-Islamiya, which has attacked police, tourists and Christians in a war to install an Islamic state. Abdel-Rahman was acquitted of inciting the assassination of President Anwar Sadat in 1981.
